situation:
You are the customer relations manager for PENFIELD OFFICE SUPPLY, a forty-year-old chain selling paper, furniture and equipment to schools, clinics and small offices. The owner (judge) has asked you to recommend how to spend the one amount the company has set aside for next winter, which is enough for only one of two plans.

A new online seller shipping from a warehouse two states away has taken business accounts for two years. January's ice storm was the first real test of the emergency plan, which closes a store when the roads are declared unsafe. Stores closed for three days, the next-day delivery the chain guarantees its accounts stopped with them, and schools and clinics ordered from the new seller.

The money can fund a winter standby program — a crew on call and two stores on generators — which keeps deliveries moving but pays off only if the heavier winters forecasters expect arrive, and is spent for nothing in a mild one. The same money can instead pay for account representatives year round, which leaves the stores closed in the next storm.

The owner (judge) wants your analysis of which use of the money will hold the chain's accounts, and of who ends up carrying the cost of that choice. The owner (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas, and will thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the owner (judge) of PENFIELD OFFICE SUPPLY. Business background is the same as the situation above.

You have asked the customer relations manager to recommend whether next winter's money goes to the standby program or to account representatives, and to tell you who ends up carrying the cost of that choice.

You will greet the participant, ask to hear their ideas, and after the presentation you will ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: Who pays for this if the winter turns out mild?
How would you explain that to the accounts it costs the most?
